cards.def: The early-nineteenth-century evangelical revival whose more optimistic view of human potential fostered mass conversions and ambitious programs for reforming individuals and society.
The conviction that divine grace brought about a new birth enabling belief in Jesus Christ, and committed the convert to reforming his or her own vices as well as the faults of others.
The doctrine that God had already determined which individuals were destined to be damned or saved and that no human effort could alter those eternal fates.
The more democratic belief that all men and women might choose and win salvation and that each individual should take an active responsibility for redemption.
A thousand years of peace and triumph that many evangelicals hoped might well begin in the United States.
The loosely united network of voluntary organizations that blanketed the United States with tracts and Bibles, missions, Sunday schools, and moral reform.
Special revival techniques Finney popularized and used systematically, including protracted meetings, praying for sinners by name, public testimony by women, and the anxious bench.
The campaign to reduce or end drinking, defended as necessary for sober voters and factory workers and as a way for women to defend the home.
The national organization that promoted abstinence from distilled liquor through thousands of local societies.
The first statewide prohibition law, which authorized search and seizure of private property and provided stiff penalties for selling liquor.
The ideal, also called true womanhood, that wives and mothers were the morally stronger "angels" of their households, confined to a private sphere apart from men's business.
A rational Christian faith, a majority only in eastern Massachusetts, that denied the divinity of Jesus while affirming humankind's ability and responsibility to follow his moral teachings.
A European-born movement that emphasized emotion and intuition as sources of truth and gloried in the unlimited potential of the individual freed from institutional restraints.
An intensely individualistic movement that sought to rise above reason and the material world, taught that every human being contained a spark of divinity, and advised, "Trust thyself."
The mid-nineteenth-century flowering of a distinctive American literature that explored nature, the individual, and the customs and character of the United States.
Planned religious or secular communities meant as model societies that would perfect human character and show the rest of the world a better way to live.
The Oneida doctrine that commune members could have sexual relations with one another, but only with the community's approval after a searching examination of the couple's motives.
The demand for an immediate end to slavery, rejecting gradual emancipation and colonization.
The strategy of convincing slaveholders, by moral argument, to renounce slavery as a sin.
An antislavery newspaper that rejected gradual emancipation, embraced immediatism, and denounced colonization.
The most successful piece of antislavery literature in the nation's history.
The belief that human beings could lead sinless lives.

The Seneca Falls statement, modeled on the Declaration of Independence, that began "All men and women are created equal" and called for educational, legal, and political rights for women, including the vote.
The House rule that automatically tabled without consideration any petition dealing with slavery.
The first antislavery political party, organized to end slavery through the political process rather than moral suasion alone.
The secret network that hid fugitive slaves and moved them northward from one station to the next.
